title: What the pandit reads
hookLine: the pandit reads and argues, but has he understood

cards: A book highlighted in yellow, page after page, the margins full of notes. Someone can quote chapter and verse, win every argument at the table, and still snap at the waiter five minutes later. Reading is one thing.
Being changed by what you read is another. The Oankar knows this gap.
It was answered, tradition says, to a pandit, a man who read and explained sacred texts, and the poem keeps turning to him with a simple question: you've read it, but have you understood?

teach.h: THE RAHAO: WHY WRITE THE TANGLES?
teach.b: The Oankar has a refrain, the line Sikhs call the rahao, the pause, where the poem stops to say what it's about. In paraphrase: listen, pandit, why write about the world's tangles?
Write the Name of the Lord, as the Gurmukh does. Notice the verb. Not stop writing.

The pandit is a man of the pen, and Nanak hands the pen back, pointed in a new direction. Elsewhere in the poem, in paraphrase: reading and reading, the pandit argues his case, but he doesn't know the treasure inside him.

That's the gap from the hook: a person can master the words of a book and never meet the One the book is about. It would be easy to hear this as a story about someone else's priest. Sikh teaching doesn't leave it there.
Guru Nanak says the same thing to every reader, and Sikh teachers turn it on their own reading of the Guru Granth Sahib. In the Asa di Var he gives a striking picture.

teach.h: CARTLOADS OF BOOKS, ONE THING COUNTS.
teach.b: In paraphrase: you could read cartloads of books, whole caravans of them, through every month and every year of your life.
Only one thing is counted; the rest is the noise of ego. The one thing is the Name, understood and lived. So the question isn't really for a pandit at a temple long ago.
It's for anyone holding a book, or a phone, today.
How much did I read is an easy question. What did it change is the hard one.

how: Sikhs speak of vichar, reflection on Gurbani, alongside reading it; study circles and katha, explanations of the hymns in the gurdwara, help listeners understand what is read.

games.q: what does “what the pandit reads” mean?
o: words he can argue but hasn't yet understood
the Gurmukhi letters children learn at school
secret texts only priests were allowed to see

games.q: what's inside what the pandit reads — tap the pairs.
p: the pause: what the poem is about
write the Name, as the Gurmukh does

s: the Oankar tells the pandit to stop writing
it tells him to write something else: the Name of the Lord.
in Sikh teaching, the warning about reading applies to Sikhs' own reading too
Guru Nanak says it to every reader, and Sikh teachers turn it on reading the Guru Granth Sahib.
in the Asa di Var, the more books read, the more counted
cartloads of books, and only one thing is counted.

games.q: you're the pandit. you can quote every line, and you win every argument. what does the Oankar's refrain ask you to do?
o: put the pen down for good.
write the Name of the Lord, as the Gurmukh does.
games.why: Nanak hands the pen back, pointed a new way: why write the world's tangles? write the Name.

practice: Choose one line you've read lately, a verse, a sentence from a book, even one from this path, and say it to yourself slowly.
Ask what it actually says, what it asks of you, and where it would make a difference, and stay with it until it feels less like information and more like something you know.
If you pray, ask for understanding; if not, let the line settle.

wordCard.voice: What the pandit reads. In the Oankar, the reader who argues but hasn't met what's inside him; the refrain hands him the pen to write the Name. Today's word.

orig.note: O pandit: how the Oankar's refrain addresses him, listen, pandit.

carryVoice: Your line: read and understand. Only one thing is counted. Go gently.
